Shock redefinition: the market-flow trigger and the MM population

One catalogue of 915 market events, defined on extreme 30-minute net taker flow. The HYPE MM population against matched non-event controls, who absorbs the flow and who the shock rule flags, and what an alternative one-sided taker rule selects instead.

WindowHYPE perpetual, 2025-03-27 to 2026-06-30 UTC
Price gatePrimary: overall-p95 absolute (168 bps). Sensitivity: weekly-relative class

Summary

Market-wide flow is absorbed broadly and carried as an inventory shock by a few already-large MMs.The median event has 115 MMs with hit-side maker volume and 5 that clear the inventory-shock bar. The five were quoting larger and closer on the side that went on to hit them: median |position| 1,753 HYPE against 253 for the rest. (§4)
A big price move is an absolute threshold.It is 168 bps, the p95 of all half-hours in the sample. Against a weekly-relative threshold it reclassifies 163 events and changes no event time. (§3)
The literature-style price-first trigger selects a different object.At matched selectivity the two triggers share a third of their half hours. The price trigger recalls 31% of the 181 roster inventory shocks against 58% for the flow trigger. Price movement and flow imbalance are not interchangeable on HYPE. (§3.4)
Matched controls turn several apparent responses into ordinary market making.911 clock-time-matched clean windows carry the same measurements. Control windows show no side lean, no shock-like inventory move and no post-event quoting shift, so what remains at events is the event. (§4)
Across all active MMs, scale predicts inventory shocks; message intensity does not.Shock rate correlates +0.63 with pre-event book size and +0.05 with trades per bin. Much of the size half is the fixed dollar floor inside the shock scale rather than behaviour; the flat activity result stands on its own. (§5.4)
A sweep and the durable price change are a second apart.The second holding a $1m sweep closes near where it opened; the price moves in the second after it, once the touch has been refilled thinly. (§6.6)
Equity is flat at the median and wide in the tails.At event end the shocked-MM median equity change is +0.14% and by +6 h +0.15%, but 9.5% of shocked wallet-events are below −5% at +6 h. Snapshots are 2 to 5.5 hours apart and cover the whole account. (§4.7)
The wallets that absorb the most flow are usually not the wallets the shock rule flags.In 38.6% of events none of the five biggest absorbers clears the bar. They make a median 48.8 times the inventory move of the event's median other MM, but they also carry the event's largest own scale, so the move is 2.2 sigma. For 73.9% of them the position never reaches 3 sigma at any minute. (§8)
A one-sided taker rule adds 327 half hours the net rule never sees, and almost none of them shock a roster MM.Matched on event count, the side-surge rule keeps 595 of the catalogue's boxes and adds 327 where both sides ran hot and the net stayed small. Those 327 contain 8 of the 181 roster shocks against 87 in the overlapping half. (§9)

Two groups of sections have their own page. Event studies holds the tick replays and the two episodes (sections 6, 7, 13 and 14). Unwinders holds the early and late split and the quoting results (sections 4.4 and 10 to 12). Section, table and figure numbers are unchanged, so a reference reads the same on every page.

Each finding shows its headline. Click one to read the explanation.

Notation and shared definitions

Symbols, subscripts and the four measurement windows, in one place

Terms used in more than one section are defined once here. Definitions that belong to a single section stay with it: the market trigger in §3.1, the population and event-time measures in §4.1, the early/late split in §4.4, the lifetime MM profile variables in §5.1.

Wallets, labels and codes

  • HYPE MM (v5d). A wallet that the v5d label model calls a HYPE market maker on a given date. The label is per date, so a wallet can be an MM on some dates and not on others, and every count of "labelled MMs" is a count on that event's date. §4 uses the actively market-making MMs defined in §4.1 and §5 the labelled MMs that pass its activity screen, with no roster restriction.
  • The roster ten. The ten HYPE market makers of the Exp7 roster, written MM01 to MM10 throughout. Exp8's original per-wallet shock catalogue was built on these ten, and the 181 roster shocks that recall and lift are scored against in §3 are its inventory shocks on those wallets. In this report the roster is a comparison reference and a source of worked examples. §4 and §5 measure the whole labelled population. §6 and §7 name roster wallets because they are the shocked MMs in those two events.
  • Wallet codes. MM01–MM10 are the roster ten. T01–T10 are the largest taker wallets of a tick replay. X01–X06 are the largest non-roster makers in the liquidation package. V01 is the largest liquidation victim. Codes are assigned inside a package and are stable within a section but not across packages — the note at the end of §7.5 explains the two event-B code sets. Roster MM, other MM and non-MM are wallet classes, not codes: other MM means labelled by v5d but not on the roster, non-MM means not labelled a HYPE MM on that date.

Fills and orders

  • Grouped fill, grouped trade. One row per taker order's execution against the book, with its level-by-level fills aggregated, from the grouped_trade_oid fill table. "Trades" counts these rows and "volume" is their USD notional, so one order that swept 200 levels is one trade.
  • Maker and taker. A fill is a taker (crossed) fill when the wallet's own order crossed the spread to take liquidity, and a maker fill otherwise. Taker share is crossed fill USD divided by all fill USD over whatever group is named.
  • ALO, IOC, GTC. Time-in-force. ALO is add-liquidity-only, a post-only order the venue rejects if it would cross; IOC is immediate-or-cancel; GTC is good-till-cancelled. "No market orders" means no unpriced immediate order was used.
  • What the order-state measures can see. Non-trigger limit orders only (ALO and GTC), from placement to their terminal status row, with right-censored orders dropped. The venue records a modify-in-place as a cancel plus a new order, so one modification counts as one cancel and one submit — which is why cancels-per-submit sits near 1 for most MMs.
  • Liquidation, ADL, forced and voluntary. A liquidation is the venue force-closing a position; ADL (auto-deleveraging) is the venue closing a position against other accounts when a liquidation cannot fill. Forced flow is liquidation plus ADL taker USD; voluntary flow is all other taker USD. A victim is the wallet whose position was force-closed, and a victim's leg is a taker leg.

Prices, clocks and windows

  • bps. One basis point is 0.01%, so 100 bps is 1%. Every bps figure is measured against the reference price named beside it; where a level matters the report gives dollars as well.
  • Strict-pre. ts_bookdiff_lt is the book state strictly before the events carried at a timestamp; ts_bookdiff_le is the state after them. Every price in §6 and §7 is strict-pre unless it is named as an after-event price. A mid quoted at a trade's millisecond is therefore the book the trade hit, not the book it left behind.
  • The 5-minute bin-label offset. Exp8 catalogue timestamps are 5-minute bin labels and the corresponding clock window is the label plus five minutes, because the 5-minute position is an end-of-bin level. §15 states the consequences; every window in §6 and §7 already carries the offset.
  • Episode. Exp8's grouping of roster shocks that overlap in time into one market episode. "Episode 89" and "episode 100" are that numbering, and one episode can contain several roster shocks.

Markouts

  • Markout Mk. For a fill at price p and size v, with d=+1 for a buy and d=−1 for a sell, Mk=d (midt+k−p) v in dollars: what the fill is worth marked to the mid k minutes later. A group of fills is quoted in bps as 104∑jMk,j/∑jpjvj, signed so that positive is favourable to the wallet. k is 30, 60 or 120 minutes, written M30, M60, M120. A negative maker markout means the mid kept moving against the side the wallet was filled on.

Replay conventions (§6 and §7)

  • W_focus. The shortest interval inside the anchor window that contains 80% of the trough-to-peak tick mid move. It is a rule, not a hand-picked window, which is why it is 212 s in event A and the whole 1,547 s leg in event B.
  • The surge-onset rule. The first second at which the 30-second rolling sum of hit-side taker USD reaches three times the trailing 6-hour p95 of that same statistic. §6.2 records why a per-second-median version cannot be used: 70% of baseline seconds carry no hit-side trade, so the median is $0 and the first ordinary trade clears the bar.
  • Baseline hour. The hour of the analysis window before the move leg opens. "Baseline-hour p95" and "baseline-hour low" are that hour's statistics, and a coin trading below its baseline-hour low is the new-low marker used in §7.3.
  • Levels swept and deepest walk. Levels swept is the number of distinct book price levels a taker order consumed. Deepest walk is the distance in bps from the strict-pre mid to the furthest level a single order reached.
  • Resting age. Time from an order's placement to the moment it was hit or cancelled. It separates a quote that was just re-armed from a stale order the price ran through, and it is the measure behind "the book that absorbed the move was seconds old".
  • Reaction latency L (Exp9's rule). Time from the taker-surge onset minute until the wallet's hit-side quoting first does either of two things: drops its resting hit-side size to 50% or less of its value at onset, or widens its best hit-side quote distance by 10 bps or more from its value at onset. Whichever fires first sets L, and L_rule records which — in both replays it was the widening. It is measured on a one-minute grid, so L is always a multiple of 60 s, and onset is searched from 15 minutes before the shock's formation start up to its peak. A larger L means the wallet left its quote in place longer.
  • Exp10's four absorption stories. Closer: the wallet's own best hit-side quote at onset is at or inside the peer median distance. Slow to pull: its L is at or above the peer median — Exp10's "did not pull" is the same test read the other way. Size: its resting hit-side size at onset is at least three times the peer median. Run through: it was filled on quotes that had been resting a long time, read off the resting-age distribution rather than from a threshold. §6.4 argues for a fifth, re-armed into the flood, for a wallet that is none of the four because it kept replacing a large near-touch quote during the move.
  • Peer median. In the replays, the median over every other MM holding a resting quote in that window — a heterogeneous set, so it shows that a wallet is extreme, not that it is extreme against its own competitor set (§9).

Statistics

  • Quantiles. A cell with three numbers is p25 / p50 / p75; where a fuller picture matters the source CSV also carries p5 and p95. A share row is a single proportion, not a quantile.
  • Spearman rho. Rank correlation, so it measures monotone association and is unaffected by the log scales these variables need. It is descriptive here and identifies nothing causal.
  • Recall, lift, Jaccard. Defined where they are first used: recall and lift against the 181 roster shocks in §3.1, bin Jaccard for two rules at matched selectivity in §3.4.

Every number on this page is measured on one of five event sets. Two are selected on market-wide taker flow and three on a wallet's own inventory, and each set marks start, peak and end on its own clock. A box under every section heading names the set and the count that section uses.

An episode is a group of set-4 shocks that overlap in time. Sets 4 and 5 carry 5-minute bin labels, and the clock time is the label plus five minutes (§15).

The 1-minute run (sets 2 and 3)

  • Run. Nt is in-direction net taker USD in minute t, and p95 is the 95th percentile of N over the 6 hours before the window. The run is the set of minutes with Nt > 0.25 × p95, with gaps of up to 3 minutes merged, and it qualifies when some minute reaches Nt ≥ 3 × p95. ts is its first minute and te its last.
  • Where the search looks. A 5-minute duration run, the run of qualifying 5-minute bins around the box, sets the stretch of minutes searched. 5-minute bins appear only there: they never select an event and never set its start or end.
  • How a run ends. Flip: the minute after te has N ≤ 0, so the opposite side took over; 74.0% of F1 runs. Fade: N stays positive but falls below the 0.25 × p95 exit bar; 19.7%. Edge: the search window ends; 6.3%.

A wallet's own clock inside an event

  • Shocked wallet-event (set-1 boxes). An active MM with |q(t1) − q(t0)| ≥ 3 sig24 over the box, where q is the exchange-reported HYPE position and sig24 the wallet's own 24-hour scale (§4.1). This is the end rule. §8 compares it with the peak rule, maxt0≤t≤t1 |q(t) − q(t0)| ≥ 3 sig24.
  • Own peak. The minute of the wallet's largest signed excursion from q(t0) inside the box. ACC runs from t0 to the own peak and UNW from the own peak to two hours after it, so two MMs in one event have different phase boundaries.
  • Recovery (sets 4 and 5). T60 is the minutes after the peak until 60% of the excursion is given back, censored at 360 minutes. §10 and §13 read the bin labels as clock times, so their windows sit five minutes early; §6, §7, §11 and §14 use clock times.

How the definition changed

  1. 2026-09-05, the catalogue of record (set 1). Events are 30-minute bins where net taker USD has |zNET| ≥ 3.70, the top 5%, giving 915 events. 5-minute bins were tested and rejected: they fire 9 to 25 times a day, and the ratio rule at 5 minutes finds roster shocks at the rate of random flags (lift 1.0). Each event's window is its 30-minute box.
  2. 2026-09-08, 1-minute anchors for the same 915 (set 2). Start and end come from a run of in-direction net flow per minute, using the 3 × and 0.25 × p95 bars. This changed the clock and kept the same events. The population rerun of that date measured the 30-minute boxes again, so every population result on this page is on set 1.
  3. 2026-09-10, side-surge families (set 3). Selection stays on 30-minute bins, but each side gets its own z. One side must surge (z ≥ 3.81 buy, 3.89 sell) and dominate the bin, and the cutoff was tuned so the count, 922, matches the 915. The plan's first 1-minute start rule, a trailing 3-minute crossing, was wrong and was dropped; the rule of record reuses the 2026-09-08 run construction.
  4. 2026-09-15, the population build on F1 (set 3). The §4 builder ran on the 922 side surges twice, on their 1-minute runs and on their 30-minute boxes; 24 of 24 checks pass. The shocked share of rows is 5.2% on the runs and 5.3% on the boxes against 5.9% on set 1, and the half hours set 1 never selects shock MMs at about half that rate (§9.7).

Which set each summary finding uses

  • Set 1, all 914 events: broad absorption and the 5 shocked MMs per event, the matched controls and equity (§4); the 25,705 absorbers that accumulated at least one own sigma and their early or late unwind (§4.4); what predicts a wallet's shock rate (§5.4); the 168 bps price gate and the class split (§3); peers taking the other side of the unwind in 45% of the events with a shocked MM (§4.8); the biggest absorbers against the wallets the rule flags (§8); quoting while unwinding, 7,492 shocked wallet-events (§12).
  • Set 3: the 327 half hours the net rule never selects, the 14-minute median run and the 74.0% flip share (§9), and the shocked-against-unshocked statistics on its own windows (§9.7).
  • Set 4: recall of the price-first and flow-first triggers (§3.4), the quote response of a shocked roster MM (§10), and the three replays: episode 89 (§6), episode 100 (§7), and episodes 39 and 47, where $1m to $9m single taker orders carry the surge (§13, §14).
  • Set 5: recovery speed as a trait of the MM, 812 shocks (§11).

1. The three axes of the shock definition

The three axes, and where each is answered

A shock definition has three axes. The size hyperparameter sets how large a move must be. The trigger is either a single MM's inventory or market-level taker imbalance. The interaction with price and equity decides whether a shock mattered. The table names the sections that answer each axis.

AxisEarlier Exp8 definitionThis reportWhere
TriggerPer-MM inventory deviation, robust z at or above 6 on the roster tenA market-level trigger from whole-market taker flow, three candidate measures compared and one recommended, a literature-style price-first trigger for comparison; then every active MM measured around those events and around matched non-event windows§3, §4
Size hyperparameterOne cutoff (|z| at or above 6, $100k floor) with a sensitivity tableThree cutoffs at two bin sizes, scored on count, composition, recall of the 181 roster shocks and information per flag; a nested strict tier§3
Price and equity interactionShock atlas: price z in the formation bin, equity at snapshotsEvery event classed big price move / liquidation cascade / no big move with an absolute gate; equity and closed PnL paths of every active MM through the event; whether BTC, ETH or SOL moved too; two tick-level replays that order price and flow in seconds§3, §4, §6, §7

The literature check (§2) sits underneath the first two axes: what the published measures are, how they are standardized, and where the cutoffs the meeting proposed sit relative to the published extreme-event standard.

2. What the literature does with order imbalance

Four things from sixteen verified references carry over to HYPE. The one that matters most for this page is the extreme-event definition, which is price-first and far tighter than the cutoffs the meeting proposed; §3.4 builds it on HYPE and compares it with the flow trigger.

The four precedents, and where our estimator departs from them
  • The ratio form is the equity standard, for one stated reason.
    Chordia and Subrahmanyam (2004) scale imbalance by total trades or total dollars "to eliminate the impact of total trading activity". Chordia, Roll and Subrahmanyam (2008) use 5-minute clock bins because shorter bins worsen buy/sell classification error. Our data carry the aggressor flag, so that reason does not apply here.
  • Extreme-event papers define the event on the price, with a percentile, and a tight one.
    Brogaard, Carrion, Moyaert, Riordan, Shkilko and Sokolov (2018) define an extreme price movement as the 99.9th percentile of the absolute 10-second midquote return per stock, report results across a range of percentiles, and note that the 99.9th percentile of trade imbalance selects almost the same sample. The meeting's cutoffs (3 sigma, top 10%, top 5%) are two orders of magnitude looser. §3.4 builds this definition on HYPE 5-minute bins and compares it with the flow-first rule.
  • The precedents support local normalization, but not our exact estimator.
    Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov (2014) and Cont, Cucuringu and Zhang (2023) estimate or depth-scale within short windows; Comerton-Forde et al. (2010) use a trailing benchmark; Easley, O'Hara, Yang and Zhang (2024) use rolling lookbacks. Exp8 is an analogue, not a replication. Same family: the normalizer is local (a trailing window, like the trailing benchmark and the rolling lookbacks) and robust to fat tails. Different estimator: those papers standardize by a within-window or trailing mean and standard deviation, not by a strictly-prior seven-day median/MAD with a dollar floor; and none of them then applies a full-sample 95th-percentile cutoff to the standardized score, which is the step that makes our event count in-sample. Median/MAD is our robustness choice for the observed fat-tailed HYPE series, not a method attributed to those papers.
  • Crypto perpetuals reverse one equity result.
    Silantyev (2019) finds trade-flow imbalance beats book-based order-flow imbalance on the BitMEX perpetual, naming thin depth and slow quote updates. That supports taker-side imbalance as the primary measure here and warns against importing an equity threshold.
Two templates for separating price-driven from flow-driven events, not yet applied

The reversal rule (more than two thirds reversed by a fixed horizon is transitory; Brogaard et al. 2018) and the state-space split of permanent (surprise order flow) from transitory (inventory) price pressure (Hendershott and Menkveld 2014). The tick replays in §6 and §7 answer the ordering question for two events directly instead.

Some items are verified to record and abstract only: the Chordia, Roll and Subrahmanyam (2002) methodology, Hasbrouck (1991), details of Menkveld and Yueshen (2019) and of Silantyev (2019), and the published venue of Easley, O'Hara, Yang and Zhang. No peer-reviewed Hyperliquid paper on order imbalance or liquidation cascades was found. One unrefereed 2026 preprint exists and is flagged as such.

3. Market taker-imbalance shocks: which measure, which cutoff, which bin

Event set 1: 915 net-flow events on 30-minute boxes. Start t0 and end t1 are the open of the first and the close of the last flagged bin; the peak is the bin with the largest |zNET|. Rules are scored against the 181 roster wallet shocks (set 4), and §3.4 builds a price-first comparison catalogue of 959 events on the same grid.

Whole-market HYPE taker flow on a clock grid. A market event is a run of bins in which net taker flow was extreme for that week. This section fixes the measure, the bin size and the cutoff, then classifies every event by what the price and the liquidation engine did. An alternative rule, built on a surge in one taker side rather than on net flow, is in §9.

Data
  • Data. Every HYPE taker fill, 2025-03-27 to 2026-06-30 UTC: 132,333 five-minute bins and 22,058 thirty-minute bins with trades, 461 dates.

3.1 Definitions

The three measures, how a flagged bin becomes an event, the three classes, and how a rule is scored

Measures per bin t (Bt, St = taker buy and sell USD in the bin)

  • Net taker flow NETt=Bt−St, in USD. The measure the catalogue is built on.
  • Imbalance ratio IMBt=(Bt−St)/(Bt+St), in [−1,1]. The equity-literature form (§2); tested and rejected below.
  • Standardized measure zX,t=Xt−med7d(X)max(1.4826 MAD7d(X), floor) for X∈{NET,IMB}: median and MAD over the seven days of bins strictly before t. This is Exp8's inventory recipe with net taker flow in place of one wallet's deviation.
Why a 7-day window and why these floors ($25,000 for NET, 0.05 for IMB)

The literature never standardizes by a full-sample sigma; every precedent is local (§2). Seven days is Exp8's window, so the two catalogues are comparable. The floors exist only to stop a division by a near-zero MAD in a dead week; the trailing robust sigma of net taker USD never falls below $87,564 at 5 minutes or $403,788 at 30 minutes, so the $25,000 floor removes 0 of 16,046 flags. A $250,000 floor would remove 14% of flags and would be a size rule in disguise.

From flagged bins to events

  • Flagged bin: |zNET,t| at or above the cutoff. The recommended cutoff is 3.70, the top 5% of all 30-minute bins.
  • Event: a maximal run of flagged bins whose NETt has the same sign, allowing one unflagged bin between two flagged ones. One flagged bin is enough to make an event; 75% of the 915 events are exactly one 30-minute bin, the longest is 180 minutes. The peak bin is the one with the largest |zNET|.
  • Hit side: the side the takers traded on (buy when NET>0). MMs absorb on the opposite side, so their inventory moves against the flow. SAME is the MM side that absorbs the takers (asks when takers buy); OPP is the other side. These two labels are used for every fill and every resting order in §4.
  • One-sided event: the hit side's taker USD per bin is at least 1.5 times its median per-bin rate over the six hours before the event, and at least twice the other side's surge multiple. Otherwise two-sided (both sides surged, or neither did). This is Exp8's rule.
Why one-sided means "1.5 times and twice the other side"

The two constants are Exp8's, kept so the label means the same thing in both catalogues. The first says the hit side really surged (half again its normal rate); the second says the surge was not matched on the other side. The share of one-sided events depends on the bin size, because a half hour is long enough for flow to come back: 54.5% at 30 minutes, 91.1% at 5 minutes, Exp8's 64.1% in between (its formation windows are 25 minutes at the median). The label must always be quoted with its bin size.

Three classes, decided in this order

  • Liquidation cascade: forced taker USD (liquidations plus ADL) is at least 10% of the event's taker USD. 41 of 915 events.
  • Big price move: the start-to-end mid move is at least 168 bps in absolute value. 168 bps is the 95th percentile of |return| over all 22,128 thirty-minute bins of the fifteen months, so "big" means "in the top 5% of all half-hours", not "big for that week". 353 of 915 events.
  • No big price move: everything else. 521 events.
Why 10% forced, why 168 bps, and why not a relative price gate

Forced share. At 5% the cascade share is 10.1% of events, at 10% it is 4.5%, at 25% 0.9%; the median event has a forced share of 0.001. Ten percent keeps the class small enough to mean "the liquidation engine was a visible part of the flow" without emptying it.

Price gate. A relative gate, maxt|price zt|≥3 with price zt=returnt/(1.4826 med7d|return|), compares each bin with its own trailing week. It misclassifies moves that were large in dollars but happened in a volatile week: 2026-06-04 06:00 fell $72.54 to $67.80 (654 bps) and is "no big move" under it. The absolute gate uses the overall distribution instead: p90 = 129 bps, p95 = 168, p99 = 271, p99.9 = 715. Under p95, 163 of 915 events change class: 139 no-big-move events become big, 24 big events become no-big-move. The big-move share is 53.6% at p90, 38.6% at p95, 15.2% at p99; p95 is used because it is the standing quantile of this project and keeps the class at a third of the sample. The relative flag is kept as a column (big_price_move) for anyone who wants "big for the week".

How a rule is scored against Exp8's 181 roster shocks

  • Recall: the share of the 181 Exp8 roster-MM inventory shocks whose formation window ([form start,peak+5 min)) overlaps an event of the rule.
  • Lift: recall divided by the recall a rule flagging the same number of bins at random would reach. Lift 1 means the rule finds roster shocks no better than chance.
  • With roster shock: the share of the rule's events that contain at least one roster shock.

The same table under the weekly-relative gate, and which events flip

Under the relative gate (max|price z|≥3) the cells are big price move 120 + 118, cascade 12 + 29 and no big move 367 + 269. Crossing the two gates: 214 events are big under both, 24 big only under the relative gate, 139 big only under the absolute gate and 497 not big under either. The 41 cascades are the same under both, because the cascade test is applied first.

  • Within the catalogue, a more lopsided ratio goes with a smaller price move.
    With the sign removed, the event-wide imbalance ratio and |move| correlate −0.23 at 5 minutes and −0.30 at 30 minutes, and stay negative inside a single flow direction. Standardized net dollar flow correlates +0.38 and +0.39 on the same events (Figure 2). Every event here already cleared the top-5% net-flow cutoff, so the relationship holds within the catalogue only.
Sensitivity: the weekly-relative price gate

The primary gate above is absolute: a big move is at least 168 bps, the p95 of all half-hours in the sample. The alternative calls a move big when its price z reached 3, meaning big relative to that week. Both flags are carried in the catalogue, so either can be quoted; only the label changes, never the event times.

  • The two gates disagree on 15.5% of events.
    The weekly-relative gate gives 238 big-price events, 41 liquidation cascades and 636 no-big-move; the absolute gate gives 353, 41 and 521. The 163 events that move between classes are all non-cascade.
  • The disagreement runs one way, and that is why the absolute gate is primary.
    A relative gate rescales itself in a volatile week, so a large move inside a volatile week fails it. 2026-06-04 06:00 fell 654 bps and the weekly-relative gate calls it no-big-move, because that week was volatile enough for 654 bps to be ordinary. Against the whole sample it is a big move by any reading.
  • Nothing downstream depends on the choice.
    The population results in §4 are measured per event and pooled over all 915; the gate enters only where a table is split by price class.

3.4 Two shock definitions: price-first and flow-first

The recommended rule is flow-first. The literature's extreme-event definition is price-first: Brogaard, Carrion, Moyaert, Riordan, Shkilko and Sokolov (2018) call an extreme price movement any 10-second interval whose absolute midquote return is in the top 0.1% for that stock, and report that the top 0.1% of trade imbalances picks almost the same intervals. Do a price trigger and a flow trigger pick the same half hours on HYPE? Each price rule below flags exactly as many bins as the flow rule it is compared with, on the same grid, so the overlap is not a selectivity artefact.

How the two rules are matched: the price, volatility-scaled and flow rules, the universe and the overlap measure

Matched pairs, per grid (5-minute or 30-minute bins) and quantile q∈{90,95,99,99.9}

  • Price rule Pq: |returnt| at or above its overall q-th percentile (30-minute: 129 / 168 / 271 / 718 bps; 5-minute: 54 / 70 / 115 / 215 bps).
  • Volatility-scaled price rule PZq: |price zt| at or above its own q-th percentile, where price zt=returnt/(1.4826 med7d|return|).
  • Flow rule Fq: |zNET,t| at or above its overall q-th percentile. F95 on 30-minute bins is the recommended rule (915 events).
  • Universe: bins with both a price and a valid zNET: 21,923 at 30 minutes, 131,486 at 5 minutes. Flagged counts are identical within a pair (no ties broke the match).
  • Overlap: bin Jaccard = bins flagged by both over bins flagged by either; the chance level for two unrelated rules at the same selectivity is q'/(2−q') with q'=1−q/100, so 0.026 at q=95. Events are built from each rule's flagged bins with the §3.1 grouping rule; event overlap is the share of one rule's events that overlap in time with an event of the other.

The 5-minute 99.9th percentile is the literature's own rule transplanted to this grid: 132 bins, 124 events over fifteen months (0.27 per day), 66% one-sided, 85% clearing the 70 bps gate, 15% cascades, and 6.6% recall of the roster shocks. The paper's finding that the extreme-return and extreme-imbalance samples nearly coincide is not reproduced on HYPE: at that percentile 20% of the flow bins are also price bins.

Data holes and 2025-10-10

The market dimension's own hole flag is False everywhere, so holes were found by hand: 435 five-minute bins with no taker fills (236 on 2025-11-24, 180 on 2026-04-23) and 40 bins with a null mid at 00:00. No recommended-rule event falls on the two hole days; two events touch a null-mid bin and carry a flag. 2025-10-10 gives five events including the sample maximum (21:00 to 21:30, peak |z| 156.5, $829m of taker USD, 35% forced, four roster shocks inside); it is excluded from every pooled statistic in §4.

4. The HYPE MM population around events and matched controls

Event set 1: 914 of the 915 net-flow events on 30-minute boxes, 909 after excluding 2025-10-10 from the pooled statistics; 119,459 event × active-MM rows under the post-only-fill active rule (126,846 under the fill-based gate), each event with one clock-time-matched control window. Windows run from t0 to t1; a wallet's own peak is its largest excursion inside the box. §4.4 reads the 25,705 rows whose inventory grew by at least one own sigma on the absorption side.

Every actively market-making HYPE MM, measured around the 914 events of the §3 catalogue and around 911 clean windows matched on clock time. Which wallets absorb the flow without being flagged by the shock rule is in §8.

  • The events are the recommended market trigger of §3.
    A 30-minute bin is flagged when its net taker flow is in the top 5% of the robust score |zNET|, at or above 3.70. Grouping flagged bins gives 915 events; 914 have at least one active MM, and 909 remain once the five 2025-10-10 windows are excluded from the pooled statistics.
  • 87.1% of shocked MMs moved inventory in the absorbing direction.
    Of 7,105 shocked wallet-events, 6,186 ended the window positioned against the net taker flow (short when takers bought) and 919 moved with it. By event: in 444 of 846 events with a shocked MM every shocked MM moved in the absorbing direction, 365 were mixed, and in 37 every shocked MM moved with the flow.
  • Order-book rows cover about three quarters of the sample.
    Resting-order, distance and message-rate values exist only where the raw order store holds the wallet's orders: 72.0% of shocked, 72.2% of unshocked and 74.3% of control rows (§4.1). Fills, positions, absorption and markouts cover every row. A rebuild that reads every placement day is in progress and will replace those rows.
Sample and grain
  • Sample. 914 event windows and 911 matched controls; pooled statistics exclude 2025-10-10 and leave 909 events. Classes are the absolute price gate of §3.3.
  • Grain. One window × active-MM row; PRE2H, PRE30, the event and POST (+2 h) are kept distinct.

4.1 Definitions

Every term used in §4: windows, active MM, matched control, grain, inventory and its scale, shocked and unshocked, absorption, effective N, concentration C and direction agreement D

Windows, population, controls

  • Event window. The catalogue event's own span [t0,t1) from §3.1: one 30-minute bin for 75% of events, up to 180 minutes. Four windows are measured separately and never pooled — PRE2H is the two hours ending at t0, PRE30 the last 30 minutes before t0, EV the event itself [t0,t1), and POST the two hours beginning at t1. The reversion tail runs to t1+6 h.
  • Active MM. A wallet the v5d label model calls a HYPE market maker on that date that, in PRE2H, has at least one ALO (post-only) fill, and has at least one fill during the event. On the dates where the fill table carries no time_in_force value at all (2026-04-16 to 2026-04-22), the ALO test falls back to at least one maker fill in PRE2H. Which MMs this removes is in Table 6.
  • Matched control. Same UTC clock time and duration on a nearby date (the same clock time on day d+k, taking the nearest k in the order +1, −1, +2, −2, … that gives a clean window: 310 controls at k=+1, 131 controls at k=-1, 67 controls at k=+2, 32 controls at k=-2, 18 at |k| from 3 to 6 days), with no catalogue event in the window or in its two-hour buffers either side. Controls are matched on clock time and length only, not on volume or volatility, so an event-minus-control gap mixes "an event happened" with "the market was busy" (§9).
  • Grain. One row per window × active MM. An event's 136 active MMs are 136 rows; quantiles labelled "over window × MM rows" pool those rows, quantiles labelled "across windows" first reduce each window to one number.

Inventory, and the scale a shock is measured against

  • Position and inventory change. qt is the exchange-reported HYPE position, rebuilt from the block-ordered fill chain (not from hype_mm_5m.inventory_open_size, which drifts; §15). The event inventory change is dq=qt1−qt0, in HYPE, signed: negative means the wallet ended the window shorter than it began it.
  • Own scale sig24. sig24=max[1.4826 MAD(q−median6hq), 0.02 p95|q|, 12500/mid], with every term computed over the 24 hours before the event. It is the largest of three quantities: the wallet's robust deviation from its trailing 6-hour median position; 2% of its 95th-percentile absolute position; and the HYPE worth $12,500 at the mid at t0. The last two are floors. A shock needs |dq|≥3 sig24, so every shock is an inventory change of at least $37,500 at the start mid and at least 6% of the wallet's 95th-percentile absolute position.
  • Shocked. |zdq|=|dq|/sig24≥3. This is a label on a wallet in one window, not a property of the wallet: the same MM is shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Unshocked. An active MM in the same window that is not shocked.
  • Order-store coverage. The raw order store misses every order of some wallets on some dates. A row is covered when at least half of the orders behind its PRE2H ALO fills appear in the store. Resting-book, message-rate and order-count values exist only for covered rows; on an uncovered row they are missing, not zero. 72.0% of shocked, 72.2% of unshocked and 74.3% of control rows are covered under the existing fill-based gate.

Absorption, and how concentrated it was

  • Hit side, SAME and OPP. The hit side is the side takers traded on (the ask when net taker flow is buying). MMs absorb on that side, so their inventory moves against the flow. SAME is the MM side that absorbs the takers; OPP is the other side. Resting-order rows are averages of one-minute snapshots, not counts of events.
  • Absorption. For one wallet, its maker USD on the hit side divided by all taker USD on that side. For a two-sided event the denominator still uses the single net-flow hit side only, not both directions pooled.
  • Absorber. An active MM whose hit-side maker USD is positive. The "absorbers" column counts them; it is a participation count, not a size.
  • Absorption rank. Position in the descending order of hit-side maker USD among the window's active MMs. Rank 1 is the largest absorber during the event, not the largest MM beforehand.
  • Effective N, and what 1/HHI means. Let si be wallet i's share of labelled-MM hit-side maker USD, over the MMs with si>0. The Herfindahl index is HHI=∑isi2 and effective N is 1/HHI. Read it as a count, not an index: if k absorbers each took an equal 1/k of the hit side, then HHI=k·(1/k)2=1/k and 1/HHI=k exactly. So effective N is the number of equally sized absorbers that would produce the concentration actually observed. The median event has 115 MMs with some hit-side volume but an effective N of 15.49: the hit side was as concentrated as if only that many equally sized MMs had split it, with the rest contributing little. A single absorber taking everything would give 1; 115 identical absorbers would give 115.
  • Top-5 share. The sum of the five largest si. Effective N and top-5 share describe the same concentration from two directions and should be read together.
  • Concentration C. C=maxi|dqi|/∑i|dqi|, over the window's active MMs — the largest single wallet's share of the event's total absolute inventory displacement. C=1 means one MM carried all of it; C=1/n means all n carried equally. It is an event-level number, not a per-wallet one. Across the catalogue C never reaches 0.6 (the proposed idiosyncratic bar), so no market-level event is one MM's private problem; see §17.1.
  • Direction agreement D. D=|∑idqi|/∑i|dqi|, net over gross, again over active MMs. D=1 means every MM's inventory moved the same way, so the population as a whole took on a one-directional position; D=0 means the changes cancel exactly, so the MMs largely traded with each other and the population net is flat. D is what separates one-sided from two-sided events; C does not. The control median D of 0.52 against 0.84 at events is the single clearest event-versus-control gap in Table 7.

Timing landmarks inside the window

  • All four landmarks are minute indices on a one-minute grid with minute 0 at t0. Let s=sign(dq) and define the wallet's signed excursion at minute t as s·(qt−qt0), so a wallet building a short position has a rising excursion.
  • Own peak minute is the minute maximizing that excursion; peak excursion is the maximum itself, in HYPE, or divided by sig24 when quoted in sigma.
  • Flow peak minute is the minute with the largest hit-side taker USD. Price extreme minute is the minute of the lowest mid if the event's price move is negative, of the highest if positive.
  • Baseline is the median hit-side taker USD per minute over PRE2H — the wallet-independent "ordinary rate" for that event.

Absorbers that accumulated inventory, early and late unwinders

  • Absorption-side sign and built inventory. s=+1 when takers sell, so absorbing them makes the MM longer, and s=−1 when takers buy. The inventory built since the window start is xt=s (qt−qt0) in HYPE, read at the end of each 1-minute bin. It is positive when the position has moved toward the absorption side.
  • Accumulation A and own absorption-side peak t*. A is the largest xt over the minutes of the window, and t* is the first minute attaining it. A is reported in HYPE, in USD at the mid of the peak minute, and divided by sig24.
  • Level at the peak L. L=s (qt*−median6h q), where the median is over the six hours before t0. L is how far the peak position sits on the absorption side of the wallet's normal level.
  • Absorber that accumulated inventory. An active MM in one event with all three of: A≥sig24; L≥sig24; and absorption-side maker fills larger than all opposite-side fills over [t0,t*), both in HYPE. The last condition means the inventory was built by filling takers, not by the wallet's own crossing orders.
  • ACC and UNW for these absorbers. ACC is [t0,t*) and UNW is [t*,t*+2 h). Both are anchored on the absorption-side peak, not on the end-change direction used for shocked MMs.
  • Price extreme text. The minute of the highest 1-minute mid over [t0,t1+30 min) when the event's price move is up, and of the lowest when it is down.
  • Given back at the price extreme. G=1−xtextA, with x read at the end of the extreme minute. G=0.5 means half of A is gone. A negative G means the wallet held more than A by then.
  • Early unwinder. An absorber that accumulated inventory with t*≤text and G≥0.5.
  • Late unwinder. Every other absorber that accumulated inventory. It is late, held more than half when the own peak is at or before the price extreme and G is under 0.5, and late, peak after the price extreme when the own peak falls after it. Early and late partition the absorbers that accumulated inventory.
  • Minutes to half. Minutes from t* to the first minute with xt≤A/2. The search stops at 360 minutes, and a 360 is a censored value.

Phases and markouts

  • ACC and UNW. ACC is accumulation, from t0 to the wallet's own peak minute; UNW is unwind, from the own peak minute to two hours after it. Both are anchored on the wallet's own peak, so two MMs in the same event have different phase boundaries.
  • ACC submits / PRE2H and UNW submits / PRE2H are that phase's order submissions per minute divided by the same wallet's submissions per minute in PRE2H. A value of 1.37 means it submitted 37% more orders per minute while accumulating than it had in the two prior hours.
  • Taker share of a phase is crossing (taker) fill USD divided by all fill USD in that phase, for that wallet.
  • Markout Mk. For one fill at price p, size v, with d=+1 for a buy and −1 for a sell, Mk=d (midt+k−p) v in dollars: what the fill is worth marked to the mid k minutes later. A group of fills is reported in bps as 104∑jMk,j/∑jpjvj, signed so that positive is favourable to the wallet. k is 30, 60 or 120 minutes. Event maker M30 is that quantity over the wallet's non-crossing fills inside EV, at k=30.

Equity and closed PnL

  • Equity is the whole account across all coins, read from account-state snapshots whose cadence is 2 to 5.5 hours. A change is measured against the last snapshot in the 24 hours before t0, so "event end" spans somewhat more than the event and a value at exactly +2 h exists for under half of the wallet-events (§9).
  • Below −1% and below −5% are the shares of shocked wallet-events whose equity change is below those levels — tail counts, not quantiles.
  • Own closed-PnL baseline. A wallet-event is flagged as unusually poor when its realized closed PnL falls below that wallet's own q10 of the prior seven days. It identifies an unusual outcome, not a loss caused by the event, and exists only for wallets in the 1,035-wallet dense panel (91% of active-MM rows).
  • Major-coin range. A window is counted as having a major-coin move when BTC, ETH or SOL also traded a full-sample p90 intra-window range over the same clock window.

Every comparison in §4 is a descriptive cross-section, not a causal estimate.

  • A shocked MM was already leaning into the side that went on to hit it.
    Its median resting size on the absorption side is 1.13 times its opposite-side size over the prior two hours and 1.18 times over the prior 30 minutes.
  • The lean is in price as well as size.
    Its best absorption-side quote is 0.52 bps closer to the mid than its best opposite-side quote over the prior two hours, and 0.80 bps closer over the prior 30 minutes.
  • Control windows show no lean.
    A control inherits its side from an event that is not happening, so its two sides should be interchangeable: the resting-size ratio is 0.95 and 0.97 at the two horizons, and the best-level distances differ by 0.16 bps. Unshocked rows sit at 1.06.
  • The message loop is tilted the same way, without a withdrawal.
    Over the prior 30 minutes a shocked MM submits 1.16 times as many orders per minute on the absorption side as on the opposite side and holds a quote there in 93.3% of minutes against 86.7%. Cancels per submit is 0.985 against 0.980 in controls.
  • Only the within-wallet ratios are free of the selection effect.
    Shocked MMs rest 20 times the unshocked median size on the absorption side, and only a large book can move three of its own sigmas. Comparing a wallet’s two sides in the same window divides book scale out.

4.4 Early and late unwinders among absorbers that accumulated inventory

Timing is measured only on MMs whose inventory actually grew on the absorption side during the event. 25,705 of the 126,846 event × active-MM rows clear that bar, a median 23 per event, and they hold 64% of all hit-side maker USD. Early means half of the accumulation was already gone when the price reached its extreme.

Section 4.4 has its own page with the other unwind results: early and late unwinders →

4.5 Aggressiveness of the unwind

Shocked MMs unwind through limit orders, not by crossing the spread. 61.2% do not cross at all, and the median taker share of the unwind is 0.0%. Of those that already crossed sometimes before the event, 27.0% raise their taker share by at least 1.2× while unwinding, against 22.8% of shocked rows in control windows.

4.8 Who is on the other side of the unwind? Not the other MMs.

Unshocked MMs keep quoting through the unwind, so either they absorb it or the shocked MMs compete with each other to get out. Neither holds.

  • A median 14.4% of the shocked MMs’ unwind volume has a labelled MM on the other side
    , and 0.38% a counterparty that was itself shocked in the same event. Measured on exact taker-maker pairs over the 523 events from 2025-09-27, when the pairing table starts.
  • The median event’s shocked MMs unwind $2.00m over the two hours after their peaks.
  • Peers take the other side of the aggregate unwind in 44.8% of the 851 events with a shocked MM.
    There is no matched control for this measurement, so read it as close to a coin flip rather than as a tested null (§16). The three counterparty measures above are taken from the population build, which uses the fill-based gate, so their event counts are the ones that gate gives.

5. The MM profile: state variables across all active HYPE market makers

Population: 148 MMs, one row per MM. §5.1 to §5.3 describe lifetime state. §5.4 counts shocks as shocked wallet-events of the §4 events (set 1).

Every qualifying HYPE MM is one equally weighted observation.

Population and grain
  • Population. 148 wallets labelled HYPE MM on at least 30 dates and active on at least 10 days. An active day has at least 300 grouped trades and $1 million of HYPE notional, from 2025-03-27 through 2026-06-30.
  • Grain. The profile table has one row per MM. Population quartiles are unweighted across MMs; a high-volume wallet does not count more.

5.1 Definitions

Active bin, position, inventory volatility, deviation MAD, closed PnL per dollar and the markout rows
  • Active 5-minute bin: a bin on an active day with at least one grouped fill row. Trades count those rows; volume is their USD notional.
  • Median signed position: the median exchange-reported HYPE position over active bins. It describes the level held half the time; negative is short. Share long is the share of active bins with positive position.
  • Inventory volatility: standard deviation of the 5-minute position change, in HYPE.
  • Deviation MAD: 1.4826×median|qt−median6h(q)|, in HYPE. It is the typical distance from the MM's own recent inventory level.
  • Closed PnL per dollar: 104×∑jclosedPnLj/∑jVj, where Vj is fill USD, in bps.
  • Fill markout Mk. Defined in the notation section; positive is favourable to the wallet. The rows below apply it over a wallet’s whole active history rather than inside an event window.
  • Volume-weighted M60 and M120: sum of positive-good fill markout dollars divided by the matching fill dollars, times 104, in bps.

5.3 Inventory scale and outcomes

Spearman rank correlations (defined in §5.4), one observation per MM over the 148 wallets.

  • Deviation MAD is mostly book scale.
    Its rank correlation with median |position| is 0.94. Dividing an event inventory change by this MAD therefore asks whether it is several typical books for that MM, not whether it is large in raw HYPE.
  • Short-horizon inventory volatility is different.
    Its correlation with book size is only 0.64, and volatility as a share of the book falls sharply with book size (rho −0.89). Small books routinely turn over a larger fraction of themselves.
  • Activity is not execution skill.
    More trades do not predict better M60, and are negatively associated with closed PnL per dollar. Book size has only a weak positive relation to markouts.

5.4 Population-wide shock frequency and unwind speed

Spearman's rank correlation ρ and its test

  • ρ ranks the wallets separately on the state variable and on the outcome, then takes the ordinary correlation of the two rank lists. With no ties, ρ = 1−6∑idi2n(n2−1), where di is wallet i's rank on one variable minus its rank on the other and n is the number of wallets.
  • Reading it. ρ runs from −1 to +1. +1 means the outcome always rises with the state variable, −1 means it always falls, and 0 means the two orderings are unrelated. It measures any monotone relation, not only a straight line, and a single very large wallet cannot drive it because only ranks enter.
  • The test. p is the two-sided p-value for the null hypothesis ρ = 0: the probability of a |ρ| at least this large if the two variables were independent across wallets. It treats wallets as independent observations.

How often a wallet is shocked and how fast it recovers are governed by different traits. Book size predicts shock frequency (rho +0.51 to +0.71 across four scale measures) and message intensity says nothing about it (+0.05 and +0.11, both insignificant). For recovery speed the two swap places: activity is among the strongest predictors of a fast unwind (absorption share −0.66, trades per bin −0.38, submits per bin −0.31) while book size predicts a slow one (+0.60). Lifetime inventory volatility changes sign between the two outcomes. The wallets shocked most often are the ones that get back to half fastest (−0.24).

The size half of that result is largely a fixed dollar bar, not behaviour. The shock scale takes the maximum of three terms, and the third is a flat $12,500 / mid (§4.1). Wherever it binds, the bar is an absolute $37,500 of inventory change rather than three of the wallet’s own sigmas, and a small book can almost never clear it. It binds in 67% of the 74,189 active wallet-event rows. Where the z-score is genuinely self-relative the size result reverses: rho is +0.47 on the 462 wallets whose floor binds in over 80% of their windows, and −0.21 (p = 0.073) on the 73 wallets where it almost never binds. So “scale predicts shock frequency” is substantially “small wallets cannot clear a fixed dollar bar”. The activity result is untouched and stands on its own.
Two limits on every row. The four scale variables are close to one variable: lifetime deviation MAD against lifetime median |position| is rho +0.94. They are one fact restated, not four confirmations. And the speed outcome is heavily censored: median minutes to half is capped at 360 minutes (§4.4), and its p5 / p25 / p50 / p75 / p95 over the 223 speed-eligible wallets are 8 / 84 / 239 / 360 / 360, so above the p75 it carries ties rather than durations. Every rho is bivariate, with no controls.
Population and measurement caveats

The active-day rule deliberately removes sporadic wallets, so these 148 MMs are an active cohort rather than every address ever labelled MM. Position levels use the exchange-reported fill chain; the drifting hype_mm_5m.inventory_open_size level is not used. Correlations are descriptive and do not identify strategy or skill.

8. Who absorbs the flow, and who the shock rule flags

Event set 1: 914 of the 915 net-flow events on 30-minute boxes, 909 after excluding 2025-10-10, with 126,846 event × wallet rows. The end rule reads the position at t1; the peak rule reads it at every minute from t0 to t1.

The five wallets that fill most of the surging taker flow are usually not the wallets the shock rule flags. It flags none of them in 38.6% of events and at most one in two events out of three. The reason is the wallet's own scale: the absorbers make the largest inventory moves in the event and carry the largest sigma24, so the same move measures a median 2.2 sigma, below the threshold of 3.

Population and grain
  • Population. The 914 catalogue events with population measurements, and every active MM of each event (a fill in the 2 hours before and a fill inside the window). 126,846 event × wallet rows. Every table below excludes 2025-10-10, leaving 126,117 rows and 909 events with five ranked absorbers.
  • Grain. One row is one wallet in one event. Quantiles are unweighted across rows.

8.1 Definitions

Hit side, absorption rank, the end rule, the peak rule, and the retained fraction
  • Hit side. The taker side that surged: taker sells in a net-sell event, taker buys in a net-buy event.
  • Absorption and rank. A wallet's maker volume on the side that fills those takers, summed over the 30-minute window. absorb_rank orders the event's active MMs by it; the top-5 absorbers are ranks 1 to 5.
  • Position path. q(t) is the exchange-reported HYPE position at the end of the 1-minute bin, rebuilt from grouped_trade_oid. The level at clock time t is the bin labelled t−1 minute. t0 is the window start, te the window end.
  • Own scale. sigma24 is the wallet's own 24-hour robust inventory scale, defined in §4.1. Both rules below use the same threshold of 3.

Two rules are compared throughout this section. They differ in one place: which minute of the window the position is read at.

  • End rule, the shock rule of record (§4.1): flag the wallet when |q(te)−q(t0)|≥3×sigma24
  • Peak rule: flag the wallet when the position gets that far from the same start level at any minute of the window, maxt0≤t≤te|q(t)−q(t0)|≥3×sigma24
  • Peak excursion E is the left side of the peak rule, reported in HYPE, in USD at the mid of the peak minute, and divided by sigma24. A variant measures it from the median position of the 2 hours before the window, b=median2h(q), instead of from q(t0); 8.4 shows why that baseline is not carried.
  • Retained fraction |q(te)−b|/maxt|q(t)−b|. 1 means the position was at its furthest when the window closed; 0.3 means 70% of the largest move was already given back.

  • The unflagged absorbers make the largest moves in their event and the smallest ones relative to themselves.
    Each wallet's peak move is a median 48.8 times the median other active MM's, and in 19.5% of their rows the wallet has the single largest move of the event. Divided by its own sigma24 the same move is 2.2, under the threshold of 3.
  • The flagged absorbers are not bigger wallets; they moved further.
    Their median sigma24 is 3,655 HYPE against 4,948 for the unflagged ones, so their threshold 3×sigma24 is the lower of the two, and their median peak move is 21,501 HYPE against 10,498.
  • A sigma-scaled rank is not enough on its own.
    The unflagged absorbers still sit at the 85th percentile of their event once the peak excursion is divided by sigma24. What the rule additionally requires is that the move reach 3 sigma and survive to the last minute.

  • For 73.9% of unflagged top-5 rows the position never reaches 3 sigma24 from its start level at any minute
    (2,565 of 3,471). The other 26.1% reach it and are back under it by the window end, giving back a median 69% of the peak. The wallet's own scale is therefore the reason for three rows in four, and the round trip for the remaining one.
  • The absorbers do pass part of the flow on inside the half hour
    , and they do it through their own quotes. The median unflagged absorber holds 64% of its largest move when the window closes against 92% for the flagged ones, while its own taker share inside the window is a median 9% (6% for the flagged ones). The give-back is mostly maker fills on the other side of its book, not the wallet hitting the market.
  • The peak arrives late.
    Median minute 22 of 30 for the unflagged absorbers and 27 for the flagged ones. In three quarters of unflagged top-5 rows the peak is in the direction of the flow, meaning the wallet bought into taker selling or sold into taker buying; for the flagged rows it is 86%.

  • The peak rule adds 20 points to the top-5 flagged share and 1.5 points to everyone else.
    Events with none of the five flagged fall from 38.6% to 14.7%, and events with three or more rise from 16% to 40%. Every row the end rule flags is flagged by the start-baseline peak rule except 4 rows, 1 of them a top-5 absorber, where the two position rebuilds differ at the threshold.
  • The pre-2h baseline mixes pre-window drift into the event, so the start level is the baseline to carry.
    Of the 4,780 other-MM rows it flags that the end rule does not, 48% had already moved 2 sigma or more from their pre-2h median before the window opened, and only 27% are flagged from the start level. It also drops 769 end-flagged rows, 100 of them top-5 absorbers, whose end level is nearer the pre-2h median than their start level was.
  • A peak rule would name a shocked population 65% larger, concentrated in each event's top 20 absorbers.
    That is a description of what a different definition selects, not a recommendation: §4 and the population results downstream of it would have to be rerun on the new flag before any sentence about shocked MMs changes.
Measurement caveats

The end-minus-start change recomputed from the rebuilt 1-minute positions equals the stored dq_hype within 0.01 HYPE on 99.08% of rows. The 1,165 rows that differ do so by a median 38 HYPE, a median 0.05 of the wallet's sigma, because the two position rebuilds read the fills over different ranges. The shocked flag would change on 7 of 126,846 rows. Every table above uses the stored flag, sigma24 and dq_hype. sigma24 sits at the $12,500 floor for 52% of rows, so sigma-scaled percentiles among the small wallets carry ties rather than a ranking. Whether the 26% who reach the threshold and give it back are laying off through their own quotes or hedging in another coin is not tested here; the taker share says the exit is mostly maker fills on HYPE, but the cross-coin book is not checked.

9. Taker-surge event families: what a one-sided rule sees that the net rule does not

Event set 3: 922 side surges (F1), with 399 two-sided events (F2) and the 327 F1 events set 1 never selects (F3), against the 915 net-flow events of set 1. Selection is on 30-minute boxes; start ts and end te come from the 1-minute run, and the peak tc is the minute of largest cumulative net flow. Overlap with the 181 roster shocks is counted in §9.2.

Selecting on a surge in one taker side, at the same number of events as the net-imbalance rule of §3, keeps 595 of the catalogue's boxes and adds 327 new ones. The added events are half hours where both sides ran hot and the net stayed small, and they almost never contain a roster MM inventory shock: 8 of the 181, against 87 for the overlapping half. The three family catalogues are built; the MM outcome pass on them is not run.

Population and grain
  • Population. 1,730 target events over 2025-03-27 to 2026-06-30: 595 BOTH, 327 NEW_ONLY, 330 ZNET_ONLY, 478 TWO_SIDED. Every exhibit includes 2025-10-10 and 2026-01-31.
  • Grain. One row is one event. Quantiles are p5 / p25 / p50 / p75 / p95 over events.

9.1 Definitions

The side-surge score, the four sets, the three families, the duration run and the 1-minute anchors
  • Side-surge score. zB and zS are the §3 standardized scores computed on taker buy USD and taker sell USD separately, in place of the net measure zNET. The cutoff is set at the quantile that matches the catalogue's event count, q=0.9425, giving zB≥3.81 and zS≥3.89.
  • Dominance. A surging side is dominant when it carries at least half the bin’s taker USD and at least twice the other side’s USD in the previous bin. A 30-minute box is one-sided when a surging side is dominant, and two-sided when a side surged and no side is dominant.
  • The four sets. BOTH (595) are one-sided boxes that overlap an event of the §3 catalogue. NEW_ONLY (327) are one-sided boxes that overlap none. ZNET_ONLY (330) are §3 events no side-surge box touches. TWO_SIDED (478) are the two-sided boxes at the same cutoffs.
  • The three families. F1 = BOTH + NEW_ONLY, the 922 one-sided side-surge events. F2 = the 399 two-sided events with |I|<1/3 at the peak bin. F3 = NEW_ONLY, the 327 events the net rule never sees.
  • Duration run D, at 5 minutes: the maximal run of qualifying 5-minute bins around the box, one non-qualifying bin allowed inside, containing the window's largest same-side bin. A bin qualifies when its side score is in the full-sample top 10% at 5 minutes and the side is at least half the bin's taker USD.
  • The 1-minute anchors. Nt is in-direction net taker USD in minute t, and p95 is the 95th percentile of N over the 6 hours before the window. The run is the set of minutes with Nt>0.25×p95, gaps of up to 3 minutes merged, and it qualifies when some minute reaches 3×p95. ts is its first minute and te its last; tVp is the minute of largest same-side USD; tc is the minute at which cumulative N over the run is largest.
  • Price. ps is the mid at the first tick of ts. Mpeak is the largest in-direction mid move in bps from ps over ts to te+15 minutes, Mfinal is the move at the last mid of te+15, and ρ=Mfinal/Mpeak.
  • Big-move gate g: the full-sample 95th percentile of Mpeak for the event's length class, 153 bps for runs of 5 to 15 minutes, 195, 240 and 320 bps for the longer classes.

  • Roster inventory shocks live where the two rules agree.
    87 of the 181 shocks sit inside a BOTH box against 8 inside a NEW_ONLY box, and per bin flagged BOTH is 8.1 times random against 1.6 for NEW_ONLY. A one-sided surge that the other side answered rarely leaves a roster MM holding inventory.
  • The added events are two-way half hours, not quiet ones.
    NEW_ONLY carries $22.0m of taker USD, close to BOTH's $28.6m, but its median |imbalance| is 0.15 against 0.35 and its median box move is 91 bps against 156. Both sides ran hot in 88.7% of them.
  • The net rule keeps selecting boxes with no dominant side.
    ZNET_ONLY has a side surge at the matched cutoff in only 47.3% of its boxes and a dominance-passing bin in 38.2%, and it is the smallest set by taker USD.
  • TWO_SIDED events are the largest and the longest.
    Median $30.1m of taker USD, p95 $135.8m, and 36.0% run past one 30-minute bin.

  • The flow starts a median 8 minutes into the labelled half hour and ends a median 23 minutes in.
    22% of one-sided events start before the label and 21% end after it, so the bin boundary cuts the episode in roughly one event in five.
  • Pressure keeps building after the sharpest minute.
    tc sits a median 4 minutes after tVp, p95 21 minutes, and by the sharpest minute a median 79% of the run's cumulative net flow is already in. tc and te share the same median offset, so in most events the pressure peak is the end of the run.
  • 74% of runs end because the other side takes over
    , 20% because flow dries up, and 6% because the search window ran out. 3.5% of one-sided events have no 1-minute onset at all and fall back to the 5-minute run.
  • The two-sided episodes are not bursts.
    Their runs are a median 30 minutes long, start a median 14 minutes before the bin label, and sit a median 19 minutes before the roster wallet begins to form its position, against 2 minutes for one-sided events. Treating them as a surge at a point in time is not supported.

    Direction is close to guaranteed once the move is big enough to clear the gate.
  • Reversion is four times as common in the side-surge families as in the net-only set
    , 6.7% to 7.7% against 1.5%. The gated median one-sided event keeps 68% of its peak move 15 minutes after the run ends, with a quarter keeping under 47% and a quarter over 85%.
  • The price peak is not reliably after the pressure peak.

    The class gate passes 53.4% of F1 events, the same gate computed within the event's own date passes 59.3%, and the standing 168 bps start-to-end gate on the 30-minute box passes 37.1%. The class gate and the 168 bps gate agree on 70.5% of events; 211 F1 events peak above their class gate and give part of it back before the box ends.

    It needs one code change first: redef2_pop_common.load_all_events reads the catalogue by a hard-coded path and asserts 915 rows, so the population pipeline does not yet accept a family file. The run costs about 4 hours per family with the order stream.
  • The two-sided family needs one construction choice.
    Total taker USD is positive and right-skewed, so an exit bar at a quarter of its 6-hour p95 sits near the median of the baseline and a run on it would cover half of every window. The run measure used is the excess over the 6-hour median total, which puts a median 23% of baseline minutes above the exit bar, close to the 20% the one-sided net measure gives. The raw-total alternative is recorded per event in share_base_above_exit_rawT.

9.6 The one-sided family F1, as implemented

Side scores, the one-sided class, the 30-minute box, the 5-minute duration run, the 1-minute window, and how F2 and F3 differ

F1: one-sided side-surge events, as built by code/redef4_events.py (stage sel30) and code/redef4_steps.py (stages targets, dur5, anchor, catalog)

  • Taker flow per bin. Bt and St are HYPE taker buy and taker sell USD in 30-minute bin t (data/redef_imb_measures_30m.parquet). For side a, Vat is that side’s USD and Vot the other side’s.
  • Side score. zat=(Vat−mat)/max(1.4826 MADat, 25000), where mat and MADat are the median and median absolute deviation of Va over the 336 bins (7 days) strictly before t, with at least 40% of them observed. The $25,000 floor binds in 0 of 21,923 valid bins per side.
  • Surge flag. Aat=1 when zat≥ca. The cutoffs are the full-sample 94.25% quantile of each side’s score, cB=3.81 and cS=3.89. The quantile 0.9425 is the one that gives as many one-sided events (922) as the net-flow catalogue has (915).
  • One-sided bin. Side a is one-sided in bin t when Aat=1, Vat≥Vot and Vat≥2 Vot−1: the surging side carries at least half of the bin’s taker USD and at least twice what the other side traded in the previous bin. A bin with a surge on some side and no one-sided side is two-sided.
  • 30-minute box. Flagged bins of the same class (one-sided buy, one-sided sell) are merged into a run, with one unflagged bin allowed between two flagged ones. The box is the run’s span; its peak bin is the bin with the largest surging-side score. F1 is every one-sided box: 922 events, 439 buy and 483 sell, on 349 dates, 3 of them on 2025-10-10.
  • Duration run D, 5 minutes. Search window: the box plus one 30-minute bin on each side. A 5-minute bin qualifies when its side score (same construction on 5-minute bins, 2,016-bin trailing window) is at or above the full-sample 90% quantile, 3.33 for buys and 3.51 for sells, and Va≥Vo in the bin. D is the run of qualifying bins, one non-qualifying bin allowed inside, that contains the window’s largest same-side bin; if none contains it, the run with the most same-side USD.
  • 1-minute window. Search window: D plus 5 minutes on each side. Nt=Vat−Vot is in-direction net taker USD in minute t; p95 is the 95th percentile of N over the 360 minutes before the search window, floored at $5,000. A run is a stretch of minutes with Nt>0.25×p95, with gaps of up to 3 minutes merged. A run qualifies when one of its minutes has Nt≥3×p95; if no run does, the bar drops to 2×p95 (63 events). The primary run is the qualifying run with the largest ∑Nt. ts is its first minute and te its last. If no run qualifies at either bar (32 events), ts and te are the first and last minutes of D.
  • Event window used by the population build. [t0,t1)=[ts, te+1 min): median 14 minutes, p5 4, p25 9, p75 23, p95 38. peak_utc is tc, the minute at which cumulative N from ts is largest. The event side (hit_side) is the surging side a; the absorption side is the maker side opposite it.
  • Sets inside F1. BOTH (595): the box overlaps one of the 915 net-flow 30-minute boxes. NEW_ONLY (327): it overlaps none.
  • Classes. class3 in the population tables is the absolute price gate, as for the net-flow catalogue: liquidation cascade when forced taker USD is at least 10% of the box, otherwise big move when the box start-to-end mid move is at least 168.36 bps; F1 has 47 cascade, 314 big-move and 561 other events.

For contrast: the net-flow catalogue, F2 and F3

  • Net-flow catalogue (§3, 915 events). The same 7-day robust score computed on net taker USD Bt−St in 30-minute bins, flagged when |zNET|≥3.70, the full-sample 95% quantile. Its population windows are the 30-minute boxes (median 30 minutes, up to 180).
  • F2, two-sided (399 events). Boxes of two-sided bins at the same cutoffs (some side surged, no side passed the one-sided test), kept when |I|<1/3 at the peak bin, I=(B−S)/(B+S); 79 of 478 are dropped by that test. The 5-minute run uses a score on total taker USD B+S (cutoff 3.06) with no side condition. The 1-minute run uses the excess Xt=(Bt+St)−median6h(B+S) in place of Nt, with the same 3, 2 and 0.25 multiples of its 6-hour p95, and the direction is the sign of the run’s cumulative net flow. On all 478 two-sided candidates these runs are long: median 30 minutes, p95 96.
  • F3, side-only (327 events). The NEW_ONLY part of F1: one-sided boxes that overlap no net-flow event. Same windows as in F1.

Every row includes 2025-10-10, so the net-flow medians differ slightly from §4, which excludes it; the 914-event values with 2025-10-10 excluded reconcile with tables/redef2_pop_shocked_vs_unshocked.csv (record.md). Table 53. Resting book, messages, order counts and fills before the event, by side.

Column key and source
Cells as in Table 52. Absorption side is the maker side the event’s takers trade against, the side whose fills build the position (SAME); opposite side is the other (OPP). Rows down to traded volume are the variables of Table 9: counts, sizes, presence, submits, cancels and volume are averaged over every minute of the window with zero-quote minutes included; mean order size and the three distances are over minutes with at least one resting order on that side. Orders submitted: distinct order ids placed in the window (limit orders after the lifecycle filter of redef2_pop_orders.lifecycles: rejected, right-censored and TP/SL orders dropped). Orders live: distinct order ids resting at any point in the window. Fills: grouped_trade_oid rows of the wallet in the window; maker fills are the uncrossed ones; ALO fills have time_in_force Alo. For the net-flow catalogue orders submitted is recovered exactly as submits per minute times the window minutes and fills equal the builder’s trade count; orders live, maker fills and ALO fills were not stored in tables/redef2_pop_event_mm.csv (–). Source tables/review0915_fam_quantiles.csv, table = orders. Which rows this table uses. Every column of this table is over rows whose build date had a complete order read. redef2_pop_build.process_date reads order files for three placement days per build date, and on dates whose windows span more than that the days in between are never read, so every order placed on them is dropped as right-censored and the row carries zeros in all order-state columns. That costs the net-flow table 32,489 of its 126,846 event rows (25.6%, its control windows widen the span) and the F1 run 7,087 of 118,269 (6.0%). Fills, positions and inventory are unaffected, so Table 52 uses all rows.
