    F1 has 6,173 shocked and 112,096 unshocked rows over 922 events, with a median 125 active MMs per event against 135. Its windows are a median 14 minutes against 30.
  • On the 30-minute boxes the same events flag 5.3% of rows.
    That separates the choice of events from the length of the window.
  • |position| / own sig24, shocked against unshocked: F1 2.27 against 0.60; net-flow 2.93 against 0.59.
  • trades per bin in the prior 30 minutes, shocked against unshocked: F1 4.33 against 1.17; net-flow 3.33 against 1.00.
  • Median resting size of shocked MMs, prior 2 h, absorption side over opposite side: F1 362.6 / 273.3 HYPE (ratio 1.33); net-flow 180.8 / 157.1 HYPE (ratio 1.15).
  • Median resting size of shocked MMs, prior 30 min, absorption side over opposite side: F1 361.7 / 262.2 HYPE (ratio 1.38); net-flow 192.8 / 156.6 HYPE (ratio 1.23).
  • The half hours the net rule never sees shock MMs at about half the rate of the overlapping half hours.
    In F1 the shocked share of rows is 6.0% over the 595 BOTH events against 3.7% over the 327 NEW_ONLY events; on the 30-minute boxes 6.2% against 3.5%. That is the wallet-level reading of the roster-shock recall gap of section 9.2.
  • Absorption before and during the window separates the two groups the same way in both catalogues.
    The median shocked MM takes 0.8% of the event-side taker USD at rank 18 in F1, against 0.0% at rank 68 for the unshocked; net-flow 0.5% at rank 27 against 0.0% at rank 73.
  • Order and fill counts in the two hours before the event, median shocked against median unshocked: 3,533 against 628 orders submitted, 3,550 against 635 orders resting at some point, and 95 against 31 fills, of which 65 against 21 are on post-only orders. Submitted and live are within 1% of each other: almost every order a wallet has resting in the window was also placed inside it.
  • A quarter of the net-flow table’s order-state rows are unusable and were left out of the order tables.
    The builder reads three placement days per build date, so on dates whose windows span more than that every order placed on a skipped day is dropped and the row carries zeros in all order-state columns: 32,489 of the net-flow table’s 126,846 event rows (25.6%) and 7,087 of F1’s 118,269 (6.0%). The order tables above drop those rows for every catalogue; the state table keeps them, since fills and positions are unaffected.

15. Four things about the data that change how earlier results must be read

  1. Exp8's catalogue times are 5-minute bin labels, and the clock window is the label plus five minutes.
    The 5-minute position is an end-of-bin level, so the bin labelled 02:55 holds the position at clock 03:00, and the flow that builds a shock peaking in bin peak lives in clock [form_start + 5 min, peak + 5 min). Two independent confirmations: the tick engine reproduces Exp8's rollout_flow.hit_usd to the dollar only with the offset (without it the discrepancy is 96.7%), and the liquidation package reproduces forced_usd exactly for all three episode-100 shocks the same way. Exp9 and Exp10 anchor their windows on the labels as clock times, so their PRE window includes the first five minutes of the build and their POST1 window opens five minutes before the true peak. The size of the effect on Exp9's headline (a 1.36 bps widening of the same-side quote after the peak) has not been measured and should be, by re-running with the offset.
  2. The 5-minute grid understates fast shocks.
    MM05's 1-minute inventory trough on 2025-12-17 is −133,326 HYPE against the catalogue's −105,696 at the bin end; the amplitude is 90,151 HYPE against 62,606, so the grid is 31% low. Slow step shocks are unaffected (MM08: −947,764 against −946,977). If the size axis is re-cut, fast revert shocks should be sized on a finer grid.
  3. The dense population panel's carried inventory column is not a level.
    hype_mm_5m.inventory_open_size drifts (factor 82 for MM02); re-anchor daily to the exchange-reported close before reading a level; changes are fine (§5).
  4. Two candidate rule definitions fail on these data.
    A 3-sigma rule on the standardized imbalance ratio selects nothing because the ratio is bounded and its trailing MAD is about 0.3 (§3). A taker-surge onset defined as 3 times the trailing per-second median fires on the first ordinary trade because 70% of seconds carry no trade (§6). The replacements used here are stated in those sections and are the standing definitions for both replays.

Also recorded: the market dimension's source_hole flag is False on every HYPE bin, so the two real holes (2025-11-24, 2026-04-23) had to be found by hand; the dense panel's maker_fill_mid_distance_vw_bps is null on every date checked, so quote distances in §4 come from the raw order store.

Synthesis: what the study establishes

Quoting is broad, carrying is not

A typical event draws 115 market makers onto the side the takers hit, needs six of them to reach half the absorbed volume, and leaves five carrying an inventory shock. The five were already quoting larger and closer on that side, and control windows show no such lean. Execution capacity and balance-sheet capacity are different resources, and only the second is concentrated.

Controls turn several apparent responses into ordinary market making

Post-event activity and quote distance have to be read against the same measurements in clean windows. Where the two overlap the conclusion is ordinary variation, not strategic reaction; those nulls are kept rather than dropped. What survives the control is the direction of the population's inventory, D = 0.86 at events against 0.54 in clean windows, and the one-sided skew of a shocked MM's own book afterwards.

The event clock hides a two-stage microstructure

At the largest single ticks a taker order consumes many exact levels in one millisecond, the touch is refilled within 30 to 200 ms, and what is refilled is thin. The sweep and the durable price change are about a second apart, which no 5-minute or 30-minute measurement can see.

Absorbing the flow and being flagged for it are different measurements

The five wallets that fill most of the hit-side flow are the wallets with the largest inventory swings in normal times, so a move that is the largest in the event is a median 2.2 of their own sigma and stays under the shock rule. Reading the position at every minute rather than at the last one raises their flagged share from 23.6% to 43.6% and leaves everyone else almost unchanged, which says the rule's misses are concentrated in exactly one place. Measured on flow rather than on the flag, concentration is higher than §8's shocked counts suggest.

The trigger is stable; the price label is a choice

The 30-minute top-5% net-dollar-flow trigger defines every event in this report. Whether a move counts as big is a separate decision: against the whole sample, or against its own trailing week. Both flags are carried in the catalogue and the two disagree on 15.5% of events, so neither label overwrites the other.

What remains descriptive

Nothing here identifies a causal effect of flow on price, an optimal MM response, or skill. The label model, the event selection, snapshots 2 to 5.5 hours apart and a visible-order reconstruction that sees limit orders only set the inference boundary; §16 states it in full.

16. What this does not establish

  • Nothing here is causal.
    The catalogue records co-movement inside a bin, and the replays give an ordering in seconds on two events; a common external cause the HYPE book does not see — news, another venue, another coin — is not ruled out. The control windows say what these statistics look like in ordinary half hours, not why an event happened.
  • Two replays are two events.
    The trade-versus-cancel split, the 36-second flow lead, the fresh-quote share and the voluntary lead before the first liquidation are not shown to generalize. The same method can replay more events.
  • The flow cutoff and the price gate are in-sample quantiles.
    The trailing version of the flow cutoff exists and behaves almost identically, 921 events against 915. The 168 bps gate is the full-sample p95; a paper version should say so or use a trailing quantile.
  • One-sided against two-sided depends on the bin size
    (55% at 30 minutes, 91% at 5 minutes) and must always be quoted with it.
  • The control windows are matched on clock time and length only.
    They are not matched on volume or volatility, so an event-minus-control difference mixes "an event happened" with "the market was busy". The direction of that bias is stated where it matters in §4.
  • SAME and OPP are event-relative labels.
    For the few shocked MMs whose position moved with the takers rather than against them (about 5% of shocked wallet-events), "SAME" is still the side that absorbs the market's flow, not the side that built that wallet's position.
  • The order-state measures see limit orders only
    (ALO and GTC, non-trigger), from placement to the terminal status row, with right-censored orders dropped. Modify-in-place is recorded as cancel plus new order by the venue and counts as one cancel and one submit.
  • Equity is the whole account across all coins
    , sampled at snapshot cadence (2 to 5.5 hours), so the change "to the window end" spans more than the event, and a value at exactly +2 h exists for under half of the wallet-events.
  • The 7-day closed-PnL baseline exists only for wallets in the 1,035-wallet dense panel
    (91% of active-MM rows); the other 9% have no "worse than usual" flag.
  • Whether a shocked MM was itself liquidated is not answered here.
    Only 1 active-MM row is both shocked and liquidated outside 2025-10-10, against 28 on that day, so any split would be a reading of the crash day alone. What the sample does say is that a market cascade is not usually the liquidation of the MMs absorbing it.
  • The population profile has no held-out check
    , and every correlation in §5.4 is bivariate with no controls.
  • Peer medians in the replays are over every MM with a resting quote
    , a heterogeneous set. They show that MM05 and MM08 are extreme, not that they are extreme against their own competitor set.
  • Binding-coin attribution uses the last account snapshot
    , a median of 104 minutes old and up to 7 hours for a few large accounts.
  • The liquidation event's forced share is at the 99.94th percentile
    , so it is by construction not a typical cascade; its 361-bps move is a 98th-percentile move.
  • The counterparty test of §4.8 has no matched control.
    It is the one measurement in §4 with no control counterpart, so its 45% has no placebo baseline.

17. Decisions for Xinmeng, and open questions

Nothing below blocks the results above. Each item changes what the next build computes or how a result is labelled.

17.1 Definitions

  1. Which market trigger the paper carries. Recommended: 30-minute bins, |zNET| in its top 5% (915 events) as the working catalogue, with the 6-sigma tier (300 events) as the strict subset. The price-first trigger of §3.4 is a different object and finds roster shocks with a quarter of the lift; report it as the literature's definition applied to HYPE, not as the shock definition.
  2. In-sample or trailing cutoff. The trailing 30-day quantile costs 1.7 points of recall and changes 99 of 915 events. A referee will ask, and switching now is cheap.
  3. The price gate of record. The report uses the absolute gate (|move| at or above 168 bps, the overall 30-minute p95) and keeps the relative flag as a column. Confirm p95 against p90 (129 bps, 54% of events big) or p99 (271 bps, 15%).
  4. Whether the imbalance ratio stays in the paper. It is not a shock detector for HYPE. One paragraph as a documented negative result may still be worth it, since the meeting asked for it by name.
  5. The standing surge-onset rule and W_focus rule for replays: 3 times the trailing 6-hour p95 of the 30-second hit-side taker sum, and the shortest interval holding 80% of the trough-to-peak tick move. Both were fixed before the second replay so the two are comparable; confirm or change before a third.
  6. Idiosyncratic against systemic on the market trigger. The proposed C≥0.6 bar is unreachable (maximum 0.599); the label should live on the wallet trigger (Exp8's ALONE class) or the market-side rule should be restated on D alone.
  7. The price extreme window for the early and late split. §4.4 reads the price extreme over the event window plus 30 minutes, because the extreme of 22% of events falls on the last minute of the window. Measuring it inside the window alone moves 3,290 rows from late-held to late-peak and keeps the same label for 91.1% of rows. Confirm the 30-minute extension. A second open choice: whether the accumulation must be held for five minutes to count, which cuts the early share from 20.8% to 11.2%.
  8. Which shock scale is the one of record on the population: Exp8's level-deviation MAD with the spec floors (used) or the unit-matched MAD of 30-minute position changes, which is zero for 37% of wallet-events.
  9. Control matching. Controls are matched on clock time and length; whether to add a volume or volatility match (nearest half hour by total taker USD) before the peer-response result is quoted.
  10. Whether the start-level peak rule is carried beside the end rule (§8.5). It flags 43.6% of top-5 absorber rows against 23.6%, adds 1.5 points to every other active MM, and cuts events with none of the five flagged from 351 to 134 of 909. Carrying it as a second flag makes the shocked population 65% larger and requires rerunning §4 and everything downstream of the flag. The pre-2h median baseline is not a candidate: it mixes pre-window drift into the event.
  11. Whether the two-sided family's 1-minute extent is measured on excess total taker USD (§9.5), the construction used, or on raw total taker USD, which puts half of every window inside the run. This has to be settled before the F2 outcome pass runs.

17.2 Labels and framing

  1. MM types. Option A (carriers against flatteners on the half-life alone, transferable to the population), B (adds crossing against posting flatteners), or C (adds multi-coin against HYPE-only carriers; best separation, but MM05 sits alone). The population scatter (§5.3) shows the deviation MAD is a book-size proxy, which argues for typing on book size directly.
  2. "Shock" against "extreme event".
    The meeting's cutoffs are two orders of magnitude looser than the published extreme-event standard (99.9th percentile); §3.4 shows the two definitions select different events. The two objects need different names in the paper.
  3. A fifth absorption story.
    MM05 and MM08 were neither slow nor run through; a fast quoting loop re-armed them into the flood with two orders of magnitude more size than peers. Whether to add "re-armed" beside Exp10's closer, did-not-pull, run-through and size, and to measure it across the catalogue.
  4. A withdrawal event as its own object.
    MM05 posted no ask order for 209 seconds in the middle of the move with 213,000 HYPE of standing asks a minute earlier; this is invisible at 5-minute grain.
  5. One shock or three
    for a 533-bps grind punctuated by three forced waves: the Exp8 catalogue calls 2026-01-20 one episode with three roster shocks all peaking at 17:45, while the largest single liquidation cluster of the window (16:45, $2.54m in one millisecond) sits outside every formation window.

17.3 Follow-ups the results point to

  1. Re-run Exp9 and Exp10 with the 5-minute bin offset
    and report whether the headline quoting responses move. This is the single most consequential data item of the week.
  2. Re-anchor the dense panel's inventory level at source
    , or document the daily re-anchor as the required read pattern.
  3. Run the tick engine on 2025-08-14
    (−1,192 bps, 38% forced) as the bigger liquidation illustration, if the cross-margin question can be dropped there for want of account state.
  4. Test whether X05 and X06 leaning into forced flow is a trait.
    Two HYPE MMs put half their maker dollars on liquidation legs in the 2026-01-20 window. Whether that is stable across events is Olga's predation-versus-absorption question in its cleanest form.
  5. Joint distribution of |return| and forced share
    over all 132k 15-minute windows, to say whether the big-move and cascade axes are nearly independent.
  6. Run the MM outcome pass on the three event families
    (§9.5). It needs a small change so the population pipeline accepts a family file, then about 4 hours of compute per family with the order stream. The open sub-decision is whether the matched controls for a family exclude only that family's events or the 915 as well.

Appendix: data sources

Every result covers the HYPE perpetual on Hyperliquid from 2025-03-27 to 2026-06-30 UTC, unless its section names a narrower window.

  • Taker fills. Every HYPE taker fill, grouped by taker order with its level-by-level fills aggregated (grouped_trade_oid). Whole-market taker flow per 5-minute and 30-minute bin is built from these fills.
  • Taker-maker pairs. Each taker order's fills paired with the maker orders they filled against (trade_pairs).
  • Order store. The raw HYPE limit-order store: every placement, cancel and fill with its status rows (orders_hype and the 2026 store).
  • Tick book. The HYPE order book strictly before and after the events at each timestamp (ts_bookdiff_lt and ts_bookdiff_le).
  • Mid prices. Canonical 5-minute mids for ten coins, including BTC, ETH and SOL, used for the cross-coin checks.
  • Account snapshots. Account-state snapshots across all coins, 2 to 5.5 hours apart, from 2025-09-27: equity, positions, liquidation prices and margin mode.
  • Fills with margin state and liquidations.
    Execution-ordered fills for ten coins with the account's margin state, and the liquidation trade records.
  • MM labels. The v5d label model's per-date HYPE market-maker labels.
  • Dense MM panel. A 5-minute panel of HYPE MM fills and orders (hype_mm_5m), used for the closed-PnL baseline and for fill and submit counts. Its carried inventory level is not used (§15).
  • Exp8 roster catalogue. Exp8's frozen catalogue of 181 inventory shocks on the roster ten.

Wallets appear by code. No wallet address appears in any table or figure.
